For a one-electron species, \(\frac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^{2}\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)\).

Shortest wavelength of the Lyman series of H (\(Z = 1\)) is the series limit \(n_{2} = \infty \rightarrow n_{1} = 1\):
\[\frac{1}{x} = R(1)^{2}\left(1 - 0\right) = R \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{1}{R}.\]

Longest wavelength of the Balmer series of \(He^{+}\) (\(Z = 2\)) is the lowest-energy Balmer line, \(n_{2} = 3 \rightarrow n_{1} = 2\):
\[\frac{1}{\lambda} = R(2)^{2}\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = 4R\cdot\frac{5}{36} = \frac{5R}{9}.\]

So \(\lambda = \frac{9}{5R} = \frac{9x}{5}\).

(A) 2s: \(n = 2, l = 0 \Rightarrow\) radial \(= 2 - 0 - 1 = 1\), nodal planes \(= 0\) \(\rightarrow\) (IV) 1 radial node + no nodal plane.

Hence A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

Compare valence-electron counts and hence the Lewis dot pictures within each pair.

A: \(SO_{3}^{2-}\) has \(6 + 18 + 2 = 26\) valence electrons, so the central S carries a lone pair and the ion is pyramidal; \(CO_{3}^{2-}\) has \(4 + 18 + 2 = 24\) valence electrons, no lone pair on C, trigonal planar. NOT similar.

B: \(O_{2}^{2-}\) has \(6 + 6 + 2 = 14\) valence electrons and \(F_{2}\) has \(7 + 7 = 14\); both are a single bond with three lone pairs on each atom. Similar.

C: \(CN^{-}\) and \(CO\) both have 10 valence electrons, a triple bond and one lone pair on each atom (isoelectronic). Similar.

D: \(NH_{3}\) and \(H_{3}O^{+}\) both have 8 valence electrons, three bond pairs and one lone pair, pyramidal. Similar.

E: \(CrO_{4}^{2-}\) has \(6 + 24 + 2 = 32\) valence electrons (Cr is \(d^{0}\), all electrons paired), whereas \(MnO_{4}^{2-}\) has \(7 + 24 + 2 = 33\) valence electrons, an odd number, so Mn(VI) is \(d^{1}\) and the ion must carry an unpaired electron. NOT similar.

So A and E are the dissimilar pairs.

Work done is \(|w| = \int p_{ext}\,dV\), i.e. the area under the \(p_{ext}\)-V path.

Expansion: the gas pushes against \(p_{ext} < p_{internal}\). A single-stage expansion drops \(p_{ext}\) straight to the final pressure \(p_{2}\), giving the smallest area; a multi-stage expansion keeps \(p_{ext}\) closer to the gas pressure at every step, giving a larger area. So \(|w_{B}| > |w_{A}|\), with the reversible isothermal value as the upper limit.

Compression: the surroundings push with \(p_{ext} > p_{internal}\). A single-stage compression applies the full final pressure \(p_{1}\) over the whole volume change, the largest possible area; a multi-stage compression stays closer to the gas pressure, so it costs less. So \(|w_{C}| > |w_{D}|\), with the reversible value as the lower limit for compression.

Since every compression path lies above the reversible curve and every expansion path lies below it,
\[|w_{C}| > |w_{D}| > |w_{rev}| > |w_{B}| > |w_{A}|.\]

Hence \(|w_{C}| > |w_{D}| > |w_{B}| > |w_{A}|\).

\[x_{solvent} = \frac{n_{solvent}}{n_{solvent} + n_{solute}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.25} = \frac{1}{1.25} = 0.8.\]

So \(p = 0.8\,p^{\circ}\), i.e. the vapour pressure of the solution is \(80\%\) of that of the pure solvent.

\[\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaCl_{2}) + \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(H_{2}SO_{4}) - 2\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(HCl) = \Lambda_{m}^{\circ}(BaSO_{4}),\]

In a tetrahedral field the doubly degenerate \(e\) set \(\left(d_{z^{2}}, d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\right)\) lies at \(-0.6\Delta_{t}\) and the triply degenerate \(t_{2}\) set \(\left(d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}\right)\) at \(+0.4\Delta_{t}\). Because \(\Delta_{t}\) is small, tetrahedral complexes are high spin, so electrons fill \(e\) first (2 electrons), then \(t_{2}\) (3 electrons), then pair up.

(A) \(d^{2} = e^{2}\): CFSE \(= 2(-0.6) = -1.2\Delta_{t}\) \(\rightarrow\) (III).

(B) \(d^{4} = e^{2}t_{2}^{2}\): CFSE \(= 2(-0.6) + 2(+0.4) = -1.2 + 0.8 = -0.4\Delta_{t}\) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

(C) \(d^{6} = e^{3}t_{2}^{3}\): CFSE \(= 3(-0.6) + 3(+0.4) = -1.8 + 1.2 = -0.6\Delta_{t}\) \(\rightarrow\) (I).

(D) \(d^{8} = e^{4}t_{2}^{4}\): CFSE \(= 4(-0.6) + 4(+0.4) = -2.4 + 1.6 = -0.8\Delta_{t}\) \(\rightarrow\) (II).

Hence A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

In a tetrahedral field the ordering is inverted relative to octahedral: the \(e\) set \(\left(d_{z^{2}}, d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\right)\) is LOWER in energy and the \(t_{2}\) set \(\left(d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{xz}\right)\) is HIGHER.

(A) \(d_{xy} = d_{xz} > d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\): both \(d_{xy}\) and \(d_{xz}\) belong to \(t_{2}\) (degenerate) and lie above the \(e\) orbital \(d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\). TRUE.

(B) \(d_{xy} = d_{yz} > d_{z^{2}}\): same reasoning, both \(t_{2}\), above the \(e\) orbital \(d_{z^{2}}\). TRUE.

(C) \(d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} > d_{z^{2}} > d_{xz}\): \(d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\) and \(d_{z^{2}}\) are degenerate, not ordered, and both lie BELOW \(d_{xz}\). FALSE.

(D) \(d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} = d_{z^{2}} < d_{xz}\): correct statement of the \(e\) set lying below \(t_{2}\). TRUE.

So A, B and D only.

Boiling point is governed by the strength and extent of intermolecular hydrogen bonding, then by molar mass and surface area.

\(n-C_{4}H_{10}\) (C) has only weak dispersion forces (b.p. about \(-0.5\ ^{\circ}C\)), so it boils lowest.

\(C_{2}H_{5}NHC_{2}H_{5}\) (D), a secondary amine, has just one N-H per molecule, so its hydrogen-bonded network is limited (b.p. about \(55\ ^{\circ}C\)).

\(n-C_{4}H_{9}NH_{2}\) (B), a primary amine, has two N-H bonds and hydrogen bonds more extensively (b.p. about \(78\ ^{\circ}C\)).

\(n-C_{4}H_{9}OH\) (A) hydrogen bonds most strongly, because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen and the O-H bond is far more polar (b.p. about \(118\ ^{\circ}C\)).

Hence \(C < D < B < A\).
